system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2159-09-11 23:01:00 to 2159-09-17 17:31:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of mechanical aortic valve replacement, end-stage renal disease on dialysis, coronary artery disease, and prior right below-knee amputation was admitted for a poorly healing amputation stump with eschar. She underwent surgical debridement of the stump and VAC placement. Her INR was elevated at admission (4.3), so warfarin was held. Postoperatively, warfarin was restarted and a heparin drip was used for bridging. The VAC was changed multiple times, with good granulation tissue noted on exam. She received dialysis during the admission, with associated transient nausea managed with ondansetron. Her INR rose to 5.1 by discharge, prompting instructions to hold warfarin and follow up for INR monitoring. She was discharged home with visiting nurse support for VAC care and close outpatient follow-up.
problems: Atherosclerosis of native arteries of the extremities with gangrene
Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft
Heart valve replaced by other means
Ulcer of other part of foot

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Ms. ___, I’m Dr. ___. You came in tonight with nausea and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been feeling sick since yesterday. I couldn’t keep anything down, not even my blood pressure pills. I’ve been vomiting a few times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your blood pressure was very high when you arrived—over 250. That can definitely cause nausea. Did you miss any doses recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I try to take them, but sometimes in the evening it’s high, and then during dialysis it drops too low. I get dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll manage your blood pressure carefully here. We also noticed a small finding on your brain scan—there’s a faint spot in the medulla. It could be nothing, but we recommend an MRI to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An MRI? Is that serious? I’m already so anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s precautionary. It might be just an artifact, but we want to be sure. We’ll discuss risks and benefits with you and your husband.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT head showed that small area we discussed. The team recommends MRI, but we understand if you’re not comfortable with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: After talking with my husband, we’d rather not do the MRI. Can we just watch it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s your choice. We’ll document that and follow up with your neurologist if needed. For now, we’re focusing on your blood pressure and preparing for your planned toe surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your kidney function is stable, though your anion gap is a bit high. We think it’s from the sodium thiosulfate used in dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean something’s wrong with my dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It’s a known effect. We’ll monitor it. Your troponin is slightly elevated, but likely due to stress from vomiting and high BP, not a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re transferring you to Vascular Surgery today. They’ll manage your upcoming toe amputation. You were scheduled for a TMA, but we’ll see what’s best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the gangrene worse? I was hoping it might improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, it’s looking a bit better. We may only need to remove one or two toes instead of a larger amputation. We’ll decide in the OR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re due for dialysis today. After that, we’ll finalize plans for surgery tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on heparin again like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve started a heparin drip to keep your blood thin, especially with your mechanical valve. Your INR was low on admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After dialysis, your blood pressure spiked again. We gave IV hydralazine, and it’s coming down. The chest X-ray shows fluid in your lungs—common with volume overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I felt short of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Dialysis should help remove the extra fluid. We’ll keep monitoring your BP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had another episode of nausea and high BP this morning. We gave you a scopolamine patch and Zofran. O2 helped with the breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready for this over with. When’s the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re going to the OR in a few hours. You’ll have a left toe amputation—likely just the first and second toes. You’ll be under anesthesia and wake up in recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back. The surgery went well. You had amputation of the first and second toes on the left foot. The gangrene was limited, so we didn’t need a larger procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Is the wound okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks clean. We’ll keep an eye on it. You’re on Dilaudid for pain—we increased the dose because your foot hurt more after dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your nausea is gone, and you’re eating. BP is much better—120s over 70s—on labetalol, amlodipine, and hydralazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the new blood pressure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cardiology and Nephrology suggested switching from metoprolol to labetalol—it’s better for patients on dialysis. Hydralazine helps too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the warfarin? I was on that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We restarted Coumadin yesterday. Your INR hit 2.0, so we stopped the heparin drip. You’ll go home on warfarin—5 mg tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch for bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—watch for unusual bruising, nosebleeds, or dark stools. Your PCP will manage your INR checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound vac on the right stump was changed today—looks great with healthy tissue. Left foot wound is clean too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s healing. What about driving or walking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No driving until cleared. You can use your heel to pivot, but keep the left foot elevated when possible. No heavy lifting over 20 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but don’t soak the foot. No baths or pools for four weeks. Sutures come out in about three weeks at your vascular clinic visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re clearing you for discharge today. You’ll have home health for wound care and PT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my blood pressure meds long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cardiology suggested lisinopril instead of hydralazine, but we’ll let your nephrologist decide. You have an appointment with Dr. ___ this week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I do. And I’ll see the vascular surgeon for stitches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in about three weeks. Call if you see redness, drainage, fever, or new pain in the foot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain meds? They make me constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take them as needed. Increase fiber and fluids. We’ve included stool softeners in your instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ve set up a cardiology appointment too. Take care, and follow up closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get your discharge papers ready. The home health team will be there this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I take warfarin tonight, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 5 mg tonight. Then follow up with your PCP for INR checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Just keep up with your appointments and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m feeling much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we like to hear. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, Ms. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in with your discharge meds and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll get you out of here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy at home and keep that foot elevated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of mechanical aortic valve replacement, end-stage renal disease on dialysis, coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, and prior right below-knee amputation was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and hypertensive urgency. She presented with uncontrolled hypertension, elevated troponin likely due to demand ischemia, and an anion gap metabolic acidosis attributed to sodium thiosulfate from dialysis. A CT head revealed a nonspecific medullary hyperdensity, but the patient declined recommended MRI follow-up. She was transferred to Vascular Surgery and underwent a left first and second toe amputation due to dry gangrene, with the procedure scaled down as the gangrene had improved. Her blood pressure was stabilized with a regimen of labetalol, amlodipine, and hydralazine, and anticoagulation was bridged with heparin before restarting warfarin. She recovered well postoperatively, with controlled symptoms and a clean wound, and was discharged home with visiting nurse services for wound care and follow-up appointments in vascular surgery and nephrology.
